title: Supreme Court orders separate red warnings for high sugar, salt and fat on food packets
dek: On Constitution Day the court told the food regulator to put a separate hexagon on the front of packs for each nutrient of concern, measured on total sugars and saturated fat. Warnings become mandatory a year after the rules are notified.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday ordered India's food regulator to require warning labels on the front of packaged foods that are high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, with a separate red hexagon for each, in a 131-page judgment that rejects several parts of the regulator's own proposal and says the change is needed to protect the right to health.

A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran directed the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to measure "total sugars" and "saturated fat" rather than only "added sugar" and "added fat", to make each warning cover at least 4-5% of the main face of the pack, and to stop companies using the transition year to flood shelves with unlabelled stock. Once the rules are notified, companies will have 365 days before the warnings become compulsory.

## What happened

The judgment, written by Justice Pardiwala and dated 26 November, Constitution Day, settles an application in a public interest case brought by 3S and Our Health Society, a non-profit, which has argued since 2024 that shoppers need simple warnings at the point of sale. "The label is the only witness at the point of sale," the court wrote in its opening paragraph, asking whether that witness "will speak to every purchaser, lettered or unlettered, young or old".

The FSSAI had already accepted, in affidavits filed on 28 August and 23 September 2026, that India should adopt a warning-style label in the shape of a red hexagon. The dispute was over the details, and the court sided with the petitioner on most of them.

Single or separate warnings: the FSSAI proposed putting the words "High Sugar", "High Saturated Fat" and "High Salt" together inside one hexagon. The court said that a single hexagon "cannot possibly crowd all the words and pictures" legibly, noting that Mexico, Peru, Chile, Argentina, Colombia and Israel all use a separate symbol for each nutrient. It ordered a separate hexagon for each, carrying both the words and a standard picture of the nutrient, so that people who cannot read can still understand it.

What is measured: the regulator wanted to base the thresholds on added sugar and added fat, as used in the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians. The court ordered it to use total sugars and saturated fat, "in alignment with its own long-standing consensus", and to rework the thresholds. It said limits set too low would put warnings on almost every product and cause "label fatigue", adding that "the threshold levels presently on record fall in this category", while limits set too high would let most products escape.

Other directions: the FSSAI must fix a font size that is "prominent, conspicuous and readily legible"; publish a clear list of exempt foods with reasons; stop sweetened drinks that fall below the thresholds from using lookalike symbols; and watch for companies that swap sugar, fat or salt for additives that defeat the purpose. The Union government must enforce the 2020 rules on food sold in and around schools and teach nutrition through workshops and activities, not just textbooks.

## Background

The case has run for more than two years. In September 2022 the FSSAI published a draft "Indian Nutrition Rating" that gave packaged foods between half a star and five stars, a format the petitioner said would confuse shoppers. The regulator received more than 14,000 comments; the judgment records that consumer groups overwhelmingly favoured warning labels, while food companies largely wanted any scheme to be voluntary.

In April 2025 the court asked the FSSAI's expert committee to report within three months. After that committee reported in October 2025, a Committee of Secretaries chaired by the Cabinet Secretary recommended withdrawing the star-rating draft for lack of consensus. The regulator then proposed printing sugar, saturated fat and sodium in bold on the back of the pack, and later offered to print recommended daily limits on the front. The court said in Thursday's judgment that neither was a front-of-pack label in any real sense, and that by early 2026 "no progress worth the name had been achieved".

The court set its directions against what it called a "huge public health crisis". It cited an Indian Council of Medical Research study that estimated 101 million people in India had diabetes in 2021, 136 million were pre-diabetic and 315 million had high blood pressure. Non-communicable diseases account for roughly 63% of deaths in India each year, the judgment said, citing published research.

## Key numbers

101 million: people with diabetes in India in 2021, according to the ICMR-INDIAB study cited by the court

24% to 30.7%: rise in obesity among women between NFHS-5 (2019-21) and NFHS-6 (2023-24), as cited in the judgment; among men, 22.9% to 27.3%

4-5%: minimum share of the main face of a pack each warning must cover

365 days: transition from notification of the rules to mandatory warnings

## What they are saying

The court accepted the FSSAI's argument for a transition year, which the regulator said was needed because companies hold packaging "already printed in bulk" and because its rules must not be more restrictive of trade than necessary. The petitioner had asked for the warnings to be mandatory at once. The court said the year was reasonable but warned of "the mischief that may be played" during it, and said no further extension should ordinarily be granted.

Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi, counsel for 3S and Our Health Society, called the ruling "a landmark development in the nutritional history of the country", according to reports. Reports described the packaged food industry as having long opposed front-of-pack warning symbols; no industry body had issued a public response to the judgment by Thursday evening.

## What happens next

The FSSAI told the court it would need about four months from the judgment to finalise the draft regulations, including a 60-day public comment period at home and through the World Trade Organization, before sending them to the Health Ministry for publication. The court said the regulator must keep to that timeline and set interim deadlines for companies during the transition year.

The case will be listed again after ten weeks, when the FSSAI must file an affidavit reporting its progress. The court has kept the matter part-heard for that purpose. The FSSAI also told the court that, as a matter of policy, labelling changes come into force on 1 July, after a transition of at least 365 days from notification. On that timetable, the warnings are unlikely to become compulsory before 2028, though companies may adopt them earlier.
